core_obligations: Record the two immediate implications, from the first formulation to the second and from the second to the third (proof lines 5131).

Assume the third formulation and let a square as in the first be given; choose coverings of the relevant fibre products of formal algebraic spaces, and use quasi-compactness of the source of the square to select finitely many members whose disjoint union surjects onto it (proof lines 5131-5145).
Write out the resulting commutative diagram for each selected index and note that the maps appearing in it are given by completions of etale ring maps (proof lines 5145-5153).
Apply the first axiom to transport the property from the given factorisation to the members of the chosen coverings (proof lines 5153-5158).

Apply the second axiom twice: once with identities in place of a faithfully flat extension to reach the target of the square, and once, after passing to the finite disjoint union, to descend the property back to the morphism of the square through the faithfully flat etale cover (proof lines 5158-5189).
Apply the third axiom to pass from the property of each member to the property of their finite disjoint union (proof lines 5168-5171).
proof_roadmap: Choice of coverings and finite refinement by quasi-compactness (proof lines 5131-5145).
The commutative diagram and the identification of its maps (proof lines 5145-5153).
Applications of the three axioms in turn (proof lines 5153-5189).
difficulty_reason: For a morphism of locally countably indexed formal algebraic spaces and a local property P of morphisms of complete weakly admissible topological rings, the lemma states the equivalence of three formulations: that every commutative square of representable etale affine formal algebraic spaces over the two sides corresponds to a morphism with the property; that there is a covering of the target and, over each member, a covering of the base change such that the corresponding ring morphisms all have the property; and that there is a covering of the source with a factorisation of each member through an affine formal algebraic space etale and representable over the target such that the corresponding ring morphism has the property (statement lines 5103-5129). Two of the three implications are immediate, and the substance is the step from the third formulation to the first, which is a finite chase through the locality axioms. Given a square as in the first formulation, coverings of the relevant fibre products are chosen, quasi-compactness of the source of the square is used to select finitely many members of one of them so that the resulting disjoint union surjects onto it, and then the three axioms are applied in turn: the first to transport the property along the completions of etale ring maps appearing in the diagram, the second twice, once with identities standing in for the surjective flat map and once at the end with a degenerate extension, and the third to pass to the finite disjoint union, after which the surjectivity of the covering morphism is converted into a faithfully flat etale ring map whose completion carries the property back to the morphism of the square by the second axiom (proof lines 5131-5189). The claim is H2: the argument is a single chase, but each of its four moves -- choosing the finite refinement by quasi-compactness, and applying the three axioms at the points where their hypotheses hold -- has to be justified against the statements of the axioms.
